intro: Seventeen bars: four groups of four, then a held chord. On the page the marks are p and pp with a single hairpin, so most of the shaping you hear is the pianist’s own. Listen for the final chord, which does not answer.
question: Can a piece end on a question?

cues.title: Chords over single bass notes
cues.text: In two beats to the bar the right hand plays chord figures in semiquavers marked p, while the left hand answers each with one bass note and a rest. By the third bar the mark is pp. The bass begins on an A.
cues.evidence: First edition p. 7 (IMSLP #03060): 2/4, p in bar 1, pp in bar 3, chord figures over single bass notes and rests. Report: bass on A at 0:00 and 0:05, level −12.3 dB at 0:00 then −17.6 dB at 0:05.
cues.how: Placed from the score’s proportions; the timing is approximate.

cues.title: Four-bar groups, one every eighteen seconds
cues.text: Double bars close the groups after bars 4 and 8. The recording’s boundaries fall at about 0:18, 0:36 and 0:54, so each group of four bars takes about eighteen seconds. Ritardando marks begin only in the third group.
cues.evidence: Report: novelty 0.97 at 0:18, 1.00 at 0:36, 0.66 at 0:54. Score p. 7: double bars after bars 4 and 8; the first ritardando is written over bar 9. The count of 17 bars is from the page.

cues.title: The loudest stretch is the pianist’s choice
cues.text: The page asks only for p and pp, with one hairpin. In the recording the relative level still rises, with its loudest windows at 0:35 and 0:45. Notice how much shaping a quiet piece allows.
cues.evidence: Report: loudest windows 0:35 (−8.8 dB) and 0:45 (−10.5 dB) against −17.6 to −20.8 dB at 0:05–0:15. Dynamic marks on p. 7 are p and pp, with one hairpin in the third system; the report’s levels are relative within this recording, not dynamics.

cues.title: Liszt’s copy, and a puzzle of tempo
cues.text: Schumann inscribed an early printing “to F. Liszt in friendship”, Vienna, 13 March 1839, and wrote Langsam — slowly — above this piece by hand. That copy has no metronome marks; the later issue gives a quaver mark above 100, at which these bars would last about half a minute.
cues.evidence: Zwickau catalogue, items 7–8: Liszt copy without the later metronome figures, with a handwritten “Langsam” for Bittendes Kind; the second issue added metronome marks. Page 7 prints a quaver mark with a three-digit figure above 100; 17 bars of four quavers at that pace is about 26–30 s. This recording takes 83 s. Michael Struck (Henle blog) says Schumann did not supply the marks but let them pass uncorrected.

cues.title: The last chord leaves the question open
cues.text: The final bar is a held chord with a fermata after the last slowing. The bass is an A again, the dominant of the D-major key signature, and the sound falls from −21 dB at 1:00 to near silence by 1:20.
cues.evidence: Report: level −21.0 dB at 1:00, −32.2 dB at 1:15, −40.9 dB at 1:20; onsets 0.6 per second at 1:10 and 0.2 at 1:15; bass on A and top pitch classes A E C♯ at 1:15–1:20. Score p. 7: ritardando and a fermata over the final chord; key signature of two sharps.

transitions.title: A double bar, then the chords begin again
transitions.how: The first group closes at a double bar. The next begins with the same kind of chord figure over a single bass note, again marked p, and the second group answers the first at a new pitch level. Metre and texture are unchanged, so the repetition sounds like a request made again, not a new idea.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.97 at 0:18; level rising from −20.8 dB at 0:15 to −10.5 dB at 0:20. Score p. 7: double bar after bar 4 and p over the figure that follows.

transitions.title: The first ritardando, and the loudest point
transitions.how: A second double bar, after bar 8, leads to the group where the first ritardando is written, over bars 9–10, with a short hairpin and p. The bass moves to B here rather than A. In this recording the relative level reaches its highest windows around this group; the score stays at p and pp, so the climax is one of touch and pacing.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 1.00 at 0:36, loudest window 0:35 (−8.8 dB), bass on B at 0:30–0:40. Score p. 7: double bar after bar 8, ri-tar-dan-do over bars 9–10, a hairpin and p in the third system.

transitions.title: Slowing twice before the final group
transitions.how: The score marks a second ritardando over bars 11–12 and a third over bars 15–16. The dynamic stays at pp and no later swell is written, so the energy ebbs towards the closing chord rather than building to a climax.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.66 at 0:54; level falling from −10.5 dB at 0:45 to −21.0 dB at 1:00. Score p. 7, fourth and fifth systems: three ritardando marks in all, pp.

transitions.title: A fermata on the dominant
transitions.how: After the last ritardando the final bar is a chord held under a fermata. Its bass is an A, the dominant of the D-major key signature, so the piece ends on harmony that normally expects a resolution and the plea is left open.
transitions.evidence: Report: novelty 0.42 at 1:08; onsets fall from 1.2 per second at 1:05 to 0.2 at 1:15; bass on A and pitch classes A E C♯ at 1:15–1:20. Score p. 7: fermata over the final chord; two-sharp key signature.

facts: Piano with Friedrich Wieck; composition with Heinrich Dorn; extensive private study of Bach and Beethoven
Co-founder of the Neue Zeitschrift für Musik, 1834; editor until 1844
Married Clara Wieck in 1840; eight children, seven surviving infancy
Leipzig Conservatoire teacher; municipal music director, Düsseldorf, 1850–53
composer.background:
Schumann grew up in Zwickau, where his father August was a bookseller and publisher. Reading and music developed together: Jean Paul’s novels, with their interruptions, doubles and changes of narrative voice, mattered alongside piano lessons. Sent to Leipzig to study law in 1828, he spent more time on music and literature; a period in Heidelberg did not reconcile him to a legal career. He returned to Leipzig to study piano seriously with Friedrich Wieck. Wieck’s daughter Clara, already performing publicly as a child, gave him an immediate example of the professional discipline he hoped to acquire.

A persistent problem with his right hand ended the prospect of a virtuoso career. The familiar account of a finger-strengthening device leaves the injury’s medical cause uncertain. Composition and criticism became his principal occupations. The early published piano works already had distinct literary and formal premises: the Abegg Variations derive a theme from letters, while Papillons relates its dances to the masked-ball ending of Jean Paul’s Flegeljahre. The miniatures’ sudden juxtapositions recreate the experience of a narrative changing speakers and levels.
composer.epithet: His music lets remembered fragments, concealed names and competing inner voices interrupt the forms that contain them.
